back: A human action that produces an incorrect result. It is committed by a PERSON (e.g., a programmer writes wrong code).
An imperfection or deficiency in a work product. It is the ERROR introduced into the code/document.
An event in which a component does not perform its required function. The DEFECT is activated and the system produces an incorrect result VISIBLE to the user.
Error (human cause) → Defect (in code) → Failure (observable symptom). A defect does not always cause a failure (e.g., dead code).
Testing shows the PRESENCE of defects, not their absence. You can never prove that software has no bugs.
EXHAUSTIVE testing is IMPOSSIBLE. You must prioritize by risk and criticality.
EARLY testing saves time and money. A defect found in requirements costs 100x less than in production.
Defect CLUSTERING: 80% of defects are usually concentrated in 20% of the code (Pareto Principle).
PESTICIDE Paradox: if you always use the same test cases, they will stop finding new defects. They must be updated.
Testing is CONTEXT dependent. You do not test a medical app the same way as an online store.
Absence-of-errors FALLACY. A bug-free system is useless if it does not meet user needs.

VERIFICATION: Are we building the product RIGHT? (vs specifications)
VALIDATION: Are we building the RIGHT product? (vs user needs)

QA: process (preventive, whole cycle)
QC: product (detective, looks for defects)
Testing: subset of QC (executing tests)
All artifacts produced during the test process: plans, test cases, test data, reports, logs, etc.

front: Testing roles: Tester vs Test Manager
back:
TESTER: designs and executes tests.
TEST MANAGER: plans, monitors, and controls the entire test process.
Tests individual components in ISOLATION. Executed by the developer. Uses stubs and drivers. Focuses on white-box.
Verifies INTERFACES between components or systems. Two types: component integration (within a system) and system integration (between systems).
Tests the complete end-to-end BEHAVIOR of the system. Verifies it meets functional and non-functional requirements. Executed in a production-like environment.
Performed by the CUSTOMER/USER to confirm the system meets their needs. Types: UAT (user), OAT (operational), alpha (internal), beta (external).

FUNCTIONAL: verifies WHAT the system does (does it work?)
NON-FUNCTIONAL: verifies HOW it does it (performance, security, usability).

WHITE-BOX: based on the internal structure of the code (tester sees the code).
BLACK-BOX: based on the specification (tester does not see the code).
Tests are written BEFORE the code. The cycle is: red (test fails) → green (minimum code to pass) → refactor. Guarantees coverage but costs more initial time.
Tests are expressed in natural language (GIVEN/WHEN/THEN) so business and technical people understand them equally. Typical tool: Cucumber.
Verifies that recent changes have NOT broken functionalities that worked BEFORE. Fundamental after any change to the software.
Verifies that a SPECIFIC defect has been fixed. The test case that originally detected it is re-executed.
Tests performed after CHANGES to the system in production. Requires impact analysis to know how much regression is needed.

STATIC: examines code/documents WITHOUT executing them (reviews, static analysis).
DYNAMIC: executes the software to find defects.
The lightest. No formal process, no defined roles, no metrics. Just a colleague reviewing. Goal: find defects quickly.
The AUTHOR guides the team through the document. Educational, builds shared knowledge. Optional moderator, optional minutes.
A technical team evaluates the product. Has a moderator, but may not have all formal roles. Oriented to finding technical defects.
The MOST FORMAL review. Has all roles: moderator, author, reviewer, scribe, reader. Follows a defined process with entry/exit. Defect metrics collected.

MODERATOR: leads and facilitates.
AUTHOR: created the document.
REVIEWER: finds defects.
SCRIBE: records defects.
READER: reads the document aloud.
Tools that analyze code WITHOUT executing it to detect bugs, standard violations, excessive complexity, etc. (SonarQube, ESLint).
Divides input data into PARTITIONS where it is assumed all values in the same group behave equally. Only ONE value per partition needs to be tested.
Tests the EDGES of partitions: the minimum and maximum of each partition. For a range [1-100]: test 1, 100 (and optionally 0, 101).
Tests the boundary AND its neighbors: min-1, min, min+1 and max-1, max, max+1. For [1-100]: test 0, 1, 2, 99, 100, 101. More rigorous.
Technique for complex logical conditions. Combines all possible combinations of input conditions with their resulting actions. Guarantees rule coverage.
Models the system as a state machine. Every TRANSITION between states is tested. Useful for systems with history-dependent behavior (ATM, login).
WHITE-BOX metric. % of executable statements that have been executed by tests. Usual goal: 100%.
WHITE-BOX metric. % of branches (TRUE/FALSE) of each decision that have been exercised. STRONGER than statement coverage.
100% Branch Coverage implies 100% Statement Coverage, but NOT vice versa. Example: an if without else can have 100% statement by only testing the true path.
The tester DESIGNS and EXECUTES tests simultaneously, based on knowledge and experience. No predefined test cases. Very useful for finding unexpected bugs.
The tester uses their EXPERIENCE to guess where defects are most likely to be. Not based on a formal technique, but on the tester's instinct.
Document describing the SCOPE, approach, resources, and schedule of testing activities. Defines: objectives, entry/exit criteria, risks, deliverables.

ENTRY (Definition of Ready): conditions that must be met BEFORE testing begins.
EXIT (Definition of Done): conditions that must be met to FINISH testing.

PRODUCT: risk that the software will fail (affects quality).
PROJECT: risk that the project will fail (delays, budget).
Prioritizes tests based on PROBABILITY of failure multiplied by IMPACT if it fails. The highest risk is tested first and most thoroughly.
Measure test progress and quality: % cases executed, % defects fixed, defect density, code coverage, etc.
Process of logging, classifying, prioritizing, and tracking defects. A defect report includes: id, description, steps to reproduce, severity, priority, status.

SEVERITY: technical impact of the defect on the system (e.g., critical, major, minor).
PRIORITY: urgency to fix from the business (high, medium, low). They may not match!
Testers independent of the developer are more effective because the author has cognitive biases preventing them from seeing their own mistakes. More independence = more objectivity.
In Agile: EVERY team member is responsible for quality. Testers collaborate with developers and business from the start.
Tools that execute tests automatically: Selenium, Cypress, Playwright (UI), JUnit, pytest (unit), Postman, REST-assured (API).
Verifies behavior under load. Types: load testing (expected load), stress testing (beyond limit), spike testing. Tool: JMeter.
Continuous Integration (CI): tests run automatically on every commit. Continuous Delivery (CD): software goes to production automatically if all tests pass.
Saves time in regression, finds defects consistently, allows running more tests, executes tests impossible to do manually (performance, load).
High initial cost, script maintenance, false positives/negatives, does not replace manual exploration, can give a false sense of security.
